note.explanation: Matter can be classified by its physical state and by whether it is a pure substance or a mixture. Chemistry is divided into branches so different kinds of substances, reactions and problems can be studied more easily. Temperature affects the solubility of many substances, and cooling a hot saturated solution can produce crystals.
examples: Cooling a hot saturated potassium nitrate solution can produce potassium nitrate crystals.
note.simple: Chemistry studies matter and its changes. Different branches focus on different kinds of matter and questions. Substances can have different structures and properties, and solubility often changes when temperature changes.
note.checkQuestion: In which state does matter exist in the Sun?
note.title: States of Matter and Phase Changes
steps: Identify the type of matter or process in the question.
Recall the relevant definition or property.
Apply it to the substance or example given.
For crystallization, dissolve the substance in hot solvent, then cool the solution.
note.answer: Matter in the Sun exists in the plasma state.

mcqs.stem: Q1.1. Matter is present in neon signs in the state of:
rationales: A neon sign does not contain a supercritical fluid.
Correct: the electric discharge ionizes the gas and produces plasma.
The gas in the sign becomes ionized when the sign operates, so the relevant state is plasma.
A neon sign does not use a liquid crystal as its light-producing matter.

mcqs.stem: Q1.2. Hazardous effects of shopping bags are studied in:
rationales: Geochemistry studies chemical processes and substances of the Earth, not primarily the effects of shopping bags.
Inorganic Chemistry studies inorganic substances and their reactions.
Analytical Chemistry identifies and measures substances, rather than focusing on environmental hazards.
Correct: Environmental Chemistry studies effects of substances and pollution in the environment.
Starch is a naturally occurring polymer.
Correct: polystyrene is a synthetic, man-made polymer.
Proteins are naturally occurring biological polymers.
Cellulose is a naturally occurring polymer in plant cell walls.

mcqs.stem: Q1.4. The crystals of which substance has rhombic shape?
rationales: Brass is an alloy, not the substance with the rhombic crystal form asked for.
Correct: sulphur can occur in rhombic crystals.
Graphite has a layered structure, not the rhombic crystal form asked for.
Bronze is an alloy, not the substance with the rhombic crystal form asked for.

options: Slaked lime used for white wash
mcqs.stem: Q1.5. Which liquid among the following is a colloidal solution?
rationales: Correct: milk is an emulsion, a type of colloid.
Slaked lime in water is a suspension rather than a colloidal solution.
Vinegar forms a true solution in water.
AgCl does not form the colloidal solution described here when simply mixed with water.

options: A solution of calcium hydroxide in water
A solution of potassium nitrate in water
mcqs.stem: Q1.6. Which of the following is a heterogeneous mixture?
rationales: A solution of calcium hydroxide in water is treated as a solution, not the heterogeneous mixture asked for.
A solution of potassium nitrate in water is homogeneous.
Hot chocolate is not the textbook example of a clearly heterogeneous mixture here.
Correct: concrete has visibly different components and is heterogeneous.

mcqs.stem: Q1.7. A state of matter whose properties are between those of liquids and crystalline solids:
rationales: Correct: liquid crystals have properties intermediate between liquids and crystalline solids.
A supercritical fluid is beyond the critical temperature and pressure, not an intermediate liquid-crystal state.
Plasma is an ionized state of matter.
Dark matter is not the state described.

mcqs.stem: Q1.8. When the tiny visible particles of a substance are dispersed through a medium, the mixture is named as:
rationales: Particles in a true solution are too small to be visible as separate particles.
Correct: a colloid has dispersed particles that are visible under suitable conditions and do not readily settle.
A suspension has larger particles that generally settle on standing.
A saturated solution describes the maximum amount dissolved at a given condition, not this type of dispersed mixture.

options: The solubility will remain the same
The solubility will first increase with temperature and then it will decrease
mcqs.stem: Q1.9. A solution of KClO₃ has a solubility of about 13.2g per 100 cm³ at 40°C. How its solubility will be affected, if you decrease the temperature?
rationales: For this solid solute, lowering the temperature decreases its solubility.
Correct: the solubility of KClO₃ decreases when temperature is lowered.
The solubility does not remain the same as temperature changes.
This option describes a change in both directions and is not what happens when temperature is decreased.

mcqs.stem: Q1.10. You are studying the rate of hydrolysis of starch under different conditions of temperature. In which branch of chemistry this topic will fall?
rationales: Organic Chemistry studies carbon compounds, but the focus here is the rate of a reaction under varying conditions.
Analytical Chemistry focuses on identifying and measuring substances.
Biochemistry studies chemical processes in living organisms; the question focuses on reaction rate and temperature.
Correct: Physical Chemistry studies reaction rates and the effect of conditions such as temperature.

written.text: Q1.1. Why is there a need to divide Chemistry into many branches? Give three reasons.
written.finalAnswer: Chemistry is divided into branches because its subject matter is vast, its study needs specialisation, and division makes the study systematic and manageable.

rubric.why: Recognises the wide scope of Chemistry.
rubric.description: State that Chemistry covers a vast range of matter and reactions.
rubric.how: Mention its vast subject matter.

rubric.why: Explains the need for focused expertise.
rubric.description: Give a reason involving specialised study.
rubric.how: Say that separate branches allow specialisation.

rubric.why: Completes the explanation and gives a useful reason for division.
rubric.description: Explain that division makes study systematic or manageable.
rubric.how: State that separate branches organise and simplify study.

modelAnswer: Chemistry has a vast scope and studies a very large number of substances and reactions.
Its division into branches allows specialisation in particular areas.
It makes the study of Chemistry systematic and manageable.

written.text: Q1.2. Reactions may take place due to electrons present outside the nucleus or they may take place inside the nucleus. Which branches of Chemistry cover these two types of reactions?
written.finalAnswer: Ordinary chemical reactions involving electrons are studied in the chemical branches of Chemistry; reactions inside the nucleus are studied in nuclear chemistry.

rubric.why: Identifies the reactions occurring outside the nucleus.
rubric.description: Name the branch area for electron-related chemical reactions.
rubric.how: State that ordinary chemical branches study these reactions.

rubric.why: Correctly identifies the study of reactions within the nucleus.
rubric.description: Name nuclear chemistry.
rubric.how: Write nuclear chemistry for nuclear reactions.

modelAnswer: Reactions involving electrons outside the nucleus are ordinary chemical reactions studied in the chemical branches of Chemistry.
Reactions taking place inside the nucleus are studied in nuclear chemistry.

written.text: Q1.3. What types of problems are solved in analytical chemistry?
written.finalAnswer: Analytical chemistry solves problems involving the identification of substances and the determination of their amounts or composition.

rubric.why: Includes qualitative analysis, which tells what is present.
rubric.description: State that analytical chemistry identifies substances.
rubric.how: Mention finding the identity of a substance.

rubric.why: Includes quantitative analysis, which tells how much is present.
rubric.description: State that it measures amounts or composition.
rubric.how: Mention determining or measuring quantity.

modelAnswer: Analytical chemistry identifies the substances present in a sample.
It also determines the amount or composition of those substances.

written.text: Q1.4. Both graphite and graphene have hexagonal layered structures. What is the difference?
written.finalAnswer: Graphite consists of many stacked layers of hexagonal carbon atoms, whereas graphene is a single layer of those atoms.

rubric.why: Identifies graphite as a structure made of many layers.
rubric.description: Describe the layered structure of graphite.
rubric.how: State that graphite has many stacked layers.

rubric.why: Gives the structural distinction that defines graphene.
rubric.description: Describe graphene as one layer.
rubric.how: State that graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms.

modelAnswer: Graphite consists of many layers of hexagonally arranged carbon atoms.
Graphene is a single layer of hexagonally arranged carbon atoms.

written.text: Q1.5. Why are supercritical fluids important?
written.finalAnswer: Supercritical fluids have useful properties between those of liquids and gases and are used as solvents and in extraction processes.

rubric.why: Shows awareness of the distinctive mixed properties of a supercritical fluid.
rubric.description: State that its properties combine liquid-like and gas-like features.
rubric.how: Mention both liquid and gas properties.

rubric.why: Explains why the material matters in applications.
rubric.description: Give a useful application or practical significance.
rubric.how: Mention its use as a solvent or for extraction.

modelAnswer: Supercritical fluids have properties between those of liquids and gases.
They are important as useful solvents and in extraction processes.

written.text: Q1.6. In which state does matter exist in the Sun?
written.finalAnswer: Plasma

rubric.why: Names the state of matter correctly.
rubric.description: Identify the state of matter in the Sun.
rubric.how: Write plasma.

modelAnswer: Matter in the Sun exists in the plasma state.

written.text: Q1.7. What is the importance of graphene?
written.finalAnswer: Graphene is important because it is very strong, light, flexible and an excellent conductor of heat and electricity, making it useful in electronics.

rubric.why: Names a significant property of graphene.
rubric.description: Give an important property.
rubric.how: Mention strength or its electrical/thermal conductivity.

rubric.why: Connects its properties with its usefulness.
rubric.description: State its importance or an application.
rubric.how: Mention its usefulness in electronics or technology.

modelAnswer: Graphene is very strong, light and flexible, and it conducts heat and electricity very well.
These properties make it useful in electronics and other advanced applications.

written.text: Q1.8. Which form of matter do most of the material things in this world belong to?
written.finalAnswer: Most material things in the world belong to the solid state.

rubric.why: Identifies the common state of material things correctly.
rubric.description: Name the form of matter.
rubric.how: Write solid state.

modelAnswer: Most material things in this world belong to the solid state.

written.text: Q1.1. How does a supercritical state look like?
written.finalAnswer: A supercritical state looks like a single uniform fluid, with no distinct boundary between liquid and gas.

rubric.why: Describes the overall appearance of the supercritical state.
rubric.description: Describe it as one uniform fluid.
rubric.how: Mention its uniform appearance.

rubric.why: Explains the key visual difference from separate liquid and gas phases.
rubric.description: State that there is no distinct liquid-gas boundary.
rubric.how: Mention the absence of a meniscus or separate phases.

rubric.why: Links the description to the asked state.
rubric.description: Identify the described matter as supercritical fluid.
rubric.how: Use the term supercritical fluid.

modelAnswer: In the supercritical state, the substance appears as a single uniform fluid.
There is no distinct boundary between its liquid and gas portions.
It does not have a separate liquid surface or meniscus.

written.text: Q1.2. In what way is plasma created in a fluorescent tube?
written.finalAnswer: An electric discharge passes through the gas in the tube and ionizes it, producing plasma.

rubric.why: Identifies the energy source that starts the process.
rubric.description: Mention the electric discharge or current.
rubric.how: State that electricity passes through the gas.

rubric.why: Names the matter in the tube that is changed.
rubric.description: Identify the gas in the fluorescent tube.
rubric.how: Mention the gas in the tube.

rubric.why: Explains how plasma forms.
rubric.description: State that the gas is ionized to form plasma.
rubric.how: Describe ionization and formation of plasma.

modelAnswer: An electric discharge passes through the gas in a fluorescent tube.
The gas becomes ionized.
The ionized gas is plasma.

written.text: Q1.3. Most of the molecules we study in biochemistry are organic in nature. Where does the difference exist in organic and biochemistry branches of Chemistry?
written.finalAnswer: Organic Chemistry studies carbon compounds, while Biochemistry studies the chemical substances and processes of living organisms, including their organic molecules.

rubric.why: Defines the subject matter of organic chemistry.
rubric.description: State what Organic Chemistry studies.
rubric.how: Mention carbon compounds.

rubric.why: Identifies the living-system focus of biochemistry.
rubric.description: State that Biochemistry concerns living organisms.
rubric.how: Mention life or living organisms.

rubric.why: Distinguishes biochemistry by its focus on chemical processes in living things.
rubric.description: Mention biological chemical substances or processes.
rubric.how: State that it studies chemical processes in living organisms.

modelAnswer: Organic Chemistry studies carbon compounds.
Biochemistry studies the chemical substances and processes in living organisms.
Thus, the difference is the focus on living systems in Biochemistry, even though many of their molecules are organic.

written.text: Q1.4. Give the reason of brilliance shown by diamond. Can you improve it?
written.finalAnswer: Diamond is brilliant because its high refractive index causes repeated total internal reflection; its brilliance can be improved by cutting and polishing it suitably.

rubric.why: Explains the optical cause of diamond's brilliance.
rubric.description: State why diamond appears brilliant.
rubric.how: Mention its high refractive index and total internal reflection.

rubric.why: Identifies the method of improving brilliance.
rubric.description: Describe how to improve its brilliance.
rubric.how: Mention suitable cutting or polishing.

rubric.why: Connects the treatment with the result.
rubric.description: State the outcome of the treatment.
rubric.how: Say that the cutting or polishing increases its brilliance.

modelAnswer: Diamond has a high refractive index.
Light undergoes repeated total internal reflection inside it, giving it brilliance.
Its brilliance can be improved by cutting and polishing it suitably to make reflecting facets.

written.text: Q1.5. Explain the dissolution of sodium chloride in water.
written.finalAnswer: Polar water molecules attract and surround Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions, overcoming the forces in the NaCl crystal and dispersing the hydrated ions through the water.

rubric.why: Identifies water's role in dissolving the ionic solid.
rubric.description: Mention the polar nature of water.
rubric.how: State that polar water molecules attract the ions.

rubric.why: Names the ions formed from sodium chloride.
rubric.description: Identify sodium and chloride ions.
rubric.how: Write Na⁺ and Cl⁻ or their names.

rubric.why: Explains how the ions leave the crystal.
rubric.description: Explain separation of ions from the ionic crystal.
rubric.how: Say water-ion attraction overcomes crystal forces.

rubric.why: Completes the explanation of the dissolved state.
rubric.description: Describe the ions dispersed in water.
rubric.how: Mention hydrated ions forming a solution.

modelAnswer: Sodium chloride consists of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions held together in a crystal lattice.
Water is polar, so its molecules attract the sodium and chloride ions.
These attractions overcome the forces holding the ions in the crystal.
The hydrated ions disperse through the water and form a solution.

written.text: Q1.6. Why do different compounds have different solubilities in water at a particular temperature?
written.finalAnswer: Different compounds have different solubilities because their particles have different structures and interact with water with different strengths.

rubric.why: Recognises that solute substances differ in their properties.
rubric.description: Mention differences in the compounds or their particles.
rubric.how: State that compounds have different structures or natures.

rubric.why: Includes the solvent in the explanation.
rubric.description: Refer to interaction with water.
rubric.how: Mention water as the solvent.

rubric.why: Explains that solubility depends on the strength of solute-water interactions.
rubric.description: Explain the different strengths of interactions.
rubric.how: State that different solute-water attractions lead to different solubilities.

modelAnswer: Different compounds have different structures and properties.
Their particles interact with water with different strengths.
Therefore, different amounts of the compounds dissolve in water at the same temperature.

written.text: Q1.7. Why NaCl can not be crystallized from water just like KNO₃?
written.finalAnswer: The solubility of NaCl changes very little with temperature, so cooling its hot saturated solution does not produce crystals as readily as it does for KNO₃.

rubric.why: Identifies the substance whose crystallization is being explained.
rubric.description: Refer to NaCl.
rubric.how: Name sodium chloride or write NaCl.

rubric.why: Gives the key difference in how NaCl solubility responds to temperature.
rubric.description: State that NaCl solubility changes very little with temperature.
rubric.how: Mention its small temperature dependence.

rubric.why: Connects low change in solubility to the crystallization comparison.
rubric.description: Explain why it does not crystallize like KNO₃ on cooling.
rubric.how: Mention that cooling yields fewer crystals than for KNO₃.

modelAnswer: The solubility of NaCl changes very little with temperature.
When a hot saturated NaCl solution is cooled, only a small amount of NaCl separates out.
KNO₃ solubility changes much more with temperature, so it crystallizes more readily on cooling.

written.text: Q1.8. Why graphite is slippery to touch? Which property of graphite enables it to be used as lubricant?
written.finalAnswer: Graphite has layers held together by weak forces, so the layers slide over one another easily; this softness and easy sliding make it useful as a lubricant.

rubric.why: Identifies the layered structure responsible for graphite's slipperiness.
rubric.description: Mention graphite's layers.
rubric.how: State that graphite has layers.

rubric.why: Explains why the layers can move.
rubric.description: Describe the weak forces between layers.
rubric.how: Mention that the layers are weakly held together.

rubric.why: States the motion that causes the slippery feel.
rubric.description: Explain that layers slide over one another.
rubric.how: Mention easy sliding of the layers.

rubric.why: Answers which property makes graphite useful as a lubricant.
rubric.description: Connect its structure to lubrication.
rubric.how: Say that easy-sliding layers let graphite act as a lubricant.

modelAnswer: Graphite has layers of carbon atoms.
The forces between the layers are weak, so the layers slide over one another easily.
This easy sliding makes graphite slippery to touch and enables it to be used as a lubricant.

written.text: Q1.1(a). Mention the name of the branch of Chemistry in which you will study each of the following topics. Rate of a reaction
written.finalAnswer: Physical Chemistry

rubric.why: Correctly classifies the study of reaction rates.
rubric.description: Name the branch that studies reaction rate.
rubric.how: Write Physical Chemistry.

modelAnswer: The rate of a reaction is studied in Physical Chemistry.

written.text: Q1.1(b). Mention the name of the branch of Chemistry in which you will study each of the following topics. Digestion of food in human body
written.finalAnswer: Biochemistry

rubric.why: Correctly classifies a chemical process occurring in a living body.
rubric.description: Name the relevant branch.
rubric.how: Write Biochemistry.

modelAnswer: Digestion of food in the human body is studied in Biochemistry.

written.text: Q1.1(c). Mention the name of the branch of Chemistry in which you will study each of the following topics. Properties of plasma
written.finalAnswer: Physical Chemistry

rubric.why: Correctly classifies the study of a state and its properties.
rubric.description: Name the branch that studies properties of matter.
rubric.how: Write Physical Chemistry.

modelAnswer: The properties of plasma are studied in Physical Chemistry.

written.text: Q1.1(d). Mention the name of the branch of Chemistry in which you will study each of the following topics. Ecosystem
written.finalAnswer: Environmental Chemistry

rubric.why: Correctly classifies the study of chemical matters in the environment.
rubric.description: Name the relevant branch.
rubric.how: Write Environmental Chemistry.

modelAnswer: An ecosystem is studied in Environmental Chemistry.

written.text: Q1.1(e). Mention the name of the branch of Chemistry in which you will study each of the following topics. Reactions taking place during fireworks
written.finalAnswer: Inorganic Chemistry

rubric.why: Correctly classifies the reactions of substances used in fireworks in the textbook branch scheme.
rubric.description: Name the relevant branch.
rubric.how: Write Inorganic Chemistry.

modelAnswer: Reactions taking place during fireworks are studied in Inorganic Chemistry.

written.text: Q1.1(f). Mention the name of the branch of Chemistry in which you will study each of the following topics. Measurement of the absorption of wavelength with the help of ultraviolet spectrometer
written.finalAnswer: Analytical Chemistry

rubric.why: Correctly classifies measurement and analysis using an instrument.
rubric.description: Name the relevant branch.
rubric.how: Write Analytical Chemistry.

modelAnswer: Measurement of absorption with an ultraviolet spectrometer is studied in Analytical Chemistry.

written.text: Q1.2. What are allotropic forms? Explain the allotropic forms of carbon and sulphur. How does coal differ from diamond?
written.finalAnswer: Allotropes are different structural forms of the same element in the same physical state. Carbon has diamond, graphite and graphene forms; sulphur has rhombic, monoclinic and plastic forms. Coal is an impure amorphous form of carbon, whereas diamond is a crystalline allotrope of carbon.

rubric.why: Defines allotropy correctly.
rubric.description: Define allotropic forms.
rubric.how: State that they are different forms of the same element in the same physical state.

rubric.why: Names the principal carbon allotropes in this chapter.
rubric.description: Give the carbon forms.
rubric.how: Name diamond, graphite and graphene.

rubric.why: Names the sulphur forms asked for.
rubric.description: Give the sulphur forms.
rubric.how: Name rhombic, monoclinic and plastic sulphur.

rubric.why: Makes the requested coal-diamond comparison.
rubric.description: Compare coal with diamond.
rubric.how: State that coal is impure/amorphous while diamond is crystalline.

rubric.why: Supplies the distinguishing material structure or purity.
rubric.description: Give the distinguishing nature of each.
rubric.how: Mention coal's impure amorphous nature and diamond's crystalline nature.

modelAnswer: Allotropic forms are different structural forms of the same element in the same physical state.
Carbon occurs as diamond, graphite and graphene.
Sulphur occurs in rhombic, monoclinic and plastic forms.
Coal is an impure, amorphous form of carbon.
Diamond is a pure, crystalline allotrope of carbon.

written.text: Q1.3. What are supercritical fluids. How are they different from ordinary liquids?
written.finalAnswer: Supercritical fluids are substances above their critical temperature and pressure, where liquid and gas are indistinguishable. Unlike ordinary liquids, they have no distinct surface or meniscus and can spread through a container like a gas while having liquid-like density.

rubric.why: Gives the conditions for the supercritical state.
rubric.description: Define the conditions of a supercritical fluid.
rubric.how: Mention conditions above the critical temperature and pressure.

rubric.why: States the defining loss of separation between liquid and gas.
rubric.description: Explain the liquid-gas nature of the state.
rubric.how: Say there is no distinct liquid-gas boundary.

rubric.why: Compares its visible behaviour with ordinary liquids.
rubric.description: Mention the lack of a distinct liquid surface.
rubric.how: State that it has no ordinary liquid surface or meniscus.

rubric.why: Adds a further contrast in its properties.
rubric.description: Give another characteristic property.
rubric.how: Mention gas-like spreading or liquid-like density.

modelAnswer: A supercritical fluid is formed when a substance is above its critical temperature and critical pressure.
In this state, the liquid and gas phases are indistinguishable and have no boundary between them.
Unlike an ordinary liquid, it has no distinct surface or meniscus.
It can spread through a container like a gas while retaining liquid-like density.

written.text: Q1.4. Define solubility of a solute. How does the solubility of solutes change with the increase in temperature?
written.finalAnswer: Solubility is the number of grams of solute that dissolve in 100 g of solvent to form a saturated solution at a particular temperature. The solubility of most solid solutes increases with temperature, while that of gases generally decreases.

rubric.why: Includes the amount of solute in the definition.
rubric.description: State that solubility is an amount of solute.
rubric.how: Mention grams or amount of solute.

rubric.why: Includes the solvent basis and saturation condition.
rubric.description: Give the usual solvent quantity and saturated-solution condition.
rubric.how: Mention 100 g solvent and a saturated solution.

rubric.why: Makes clear that solubility is specified at a temperature.
rubric.description: State that the definition is for a given temperature.
rubric.how: Include particular temperature.

rubric.why: Describes the usual temperature trends for solutes.
rubric.description: Explain how temperature affects solid and gas solubility.
rubric.how: State that most solids increase and gases generally decrease.

modelAnswer: The number of grams of solute dissolved in 100 g of solvent to make a saturated solution at a particular temperature is called solubility.
With an increase in temperature, the solubility of most solid solutes increases.
The solubility of gases generally decreases with an increase in temperature.

written.text: Q1.5. What types of movements are present in gaseous and liquid molecules?
written.finalAnswer: Molecules in gases and liquids have translational, vibrational and rotational movements; in liquids, movement is more restricted than in gases.

rubric.why: Names one molecular movement.
rubric.description: Identify translational movement.
rubric.how: Write translational movement.

rubric.why: Names a second molecular movement.
rubric.description: Identify vibrational movement.
rubric.how: Write vibrational movement.

rubric.why: Names the third molecular movement.
rubric.description: Identify rotational movement.
rubric.how: Write rotational movement.

rubric.why: Relates the movements to the two physical states.
rubric.description: Compare movement in liquids and gases.
rubric.how: Mention that gas molecules move more freely than liquid molecules.

modelAnswer: Molecules in gases and liquids have translational, vibrational and rotational movements.
Molecules move more freely in gases, while their movement is more restricted in liquids.

written.text: Q1.6. Differentiate between the areas which are studied under inorganic and organic chemistry.
written.finalAnswer: Inorganic Chemistry studies elements and their compounds other than most carbon compounds; Organic Chemistry studies hydrocarbons and their derivatives and other carbon compounds.

rubric.why: Identifies the first branch being compared.
rubric.description: Describe the area of Inorganic Chemistry.
rubric.how: Name Inorganic Chemistry.

rubric.why: States the broad subject matter of inorganic chemistry.
rubric.description: Give its subject area.
rubric.how: Mention elements and compounds other than most carbon compounds.

rubric.why: Identifies the second branch being compared.
rubric.description: Describe the area of Organic Chemistry.
rubric.how: Name Organic Chemistry.

rubric.why: States the subject matter of organic chemistry.
rubric.description: Give its subject area.
rubric.how: Mention hydrocarbons and their derivatives or carbon compounds.

modelAnswer: Inorganic Chemistry studies elements and their compounds, generally excluding carbon compounds.
Organic Chemistry studies hydrocarbons and their derivatives and other carbon compounds.

written.text: Q1.1. Preparation of solutions leads to an important process in chemistry which enables us to purify a compound through crystallization. Describe a process in which potassium nitrate is purified by crystallizing it in water.
written.finalAnswer: Dissolve impure potassium nitrate in the minimum amount of hot water, filter the hot solution, cool it to crystallize KNO₃, then filter, wash the crystals with a little cold water and dry them.

rubric.why: Starts the purification by dissolving the sample in hot solvent.
rubric.description: Explain preparation of a hot solution.
rubric.how: Dissolve the impure potassium nitrate in hot water.

rubric.why: Helps remove insoluble impurities and prepare a suitable crystallizing solution.
rubric.description: Describe making and filtering the solution.
rubric.how: Use a small amount of hot water and filter if needed.

rubric.why: Uses the temperature-dependent solubility to obtain crystals.
rubric.description: Describe crystallization on cooling.
rubric.how: Allow the hot solution to cool.

rubric.why: Separates and cleans the purified solid.
rubric.description: Describe recovery and washing of crystals.
rubric.how: Filter and wash the crystals with cold water.

rubric.why: Completes the purification procedure and identifies the product.
rubric.description: State how the purified crystals are finished.
rubric.how: Dry the potassium nitrate crystals.

modelAnswer: Dissolve the impure potassium nitrate in the minimum amount of hot water to make a hot saturated solution.
Filter the hot solution to remove insoluble impurities.
Leave the filtrate to cool so that potassium nitrate crystals form.
Filter and wash the crystals with a small amount of cold water.
Dry the purified potassium nitrate crystals.

written.text: Q1.2. Graphene is called a miracle material and it is the material of the future. Which of its many properties makes it very useful in electronics?
written.finalAnswer: Graphene is an excellent conductor of electricity and has very high electron mobility, making it useful in electronics.

rubric.why: Names the key electrical property relevant to electronic devices.
rubric.description: State its electrical conductivity.
rubric.how: Mention that graphene conducts electricity very well.

rubric.why: Adds the property that allows charge to move quickly through it.
rubric.description: State its high electron mobility.
rubric.how: Mention the high mobility of electrons.

rubric.why: Connects its properties with the application asked about.
rubric.description: State its relevance to electronics.
rubric.how: Explain that these properties make it useful in electronic devices.

modelAnswer: Graphene conducts electricity very well.
It also has very high electron mobility.
These properties make graphene very useful in electronics.

examTips: MCQs commonly test states of matter, chemistry branches, mixtures, allotropes and temperature effects on solubility.
Short questions often ask for a definition, a reason or a distinction; give the key textbook term first, then one supporting fact.

For branch-classification questions, link the topic to its focus: living systems to Biochemistry, environmental effects to Environmental Chemistry, measurements to Analytical Chemistry, and reaction rates to Physical Chemistry.
For descriptive answers, use clear comparison words such as whereas, while and because. Include named examples where asked.
For crystallization, marks are earned for the correct order: dissolve in hot water, filter, cool, separate the crystals, wash and dry.
For explanations of structure and properties, connect cause to result—for example, weak forces between graphite layers allow them to slide.

solution: Graphite has layers of carbon atoms.
The forces between the layers are weak, so the layers slide over one another easily.
This easy sliding makes graphite slippery to touch and enables it to be used as a lubricant.
yourTurn.answer: Graphite's layers are weakly held together and slide over one another easily. This property makes graphite slippery and useful as a lubricant.

steps.why: NaCl is an ionic solid, so first identify the ions present in its crystal.
steps.text: Sodium chloride consists of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions held together in a crystal lattice.

steps.why: Water is polar, so it attracts the charged ions.
steps.text: Water is polar, so its molecules attract the sodium and chloride ions.

steps.why: The solvent must pull the ions away from the crystal structure for dissolution to occur.
steps.text: These attractions overcome the forces holding the ions in the crystal.

steps.why: Once separated and surrounded by water, the ions spread through the solvent to form a solution.
steps.text: The hydrated ions disperse through the water and form a solution.

example.question: Q1.5. Explain the dissolution of sodium chloride in water.
example.answer: Polar water molecules attract and surround Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions, overcoming the forces in the NaCl crystal and dispersing the hydrated ions through the water.

explain.title: Chemistry has branches
explain.body: Chemistry covers many substances, properties and reactions. Dividing it into branches makes its study organised and allows people to specialise. Each branch focuses on a different kind of question or material.

explain.title: Matter has different states and structures
explain.body: Matter includes solids, liquids and gases, as well as states such as plasma, liquid crystals and supercritical fluids. Elements can also occur in different structural forms called allotropes, such as diamond and graphite, which are both forms of carbon.

explain.title: Mixtures and solutions are different
explain.body: A true solution is uniform, while colloids and suspensions contain dispersed particles. A saturated solution contains as much solute as can dissolve under the stated conditions.

explain.title: Solubility depends on the substance and temperature
explain.body: Different compounds dissolve to different extents because their particles interact differently with water. The solubility of most solids increases as temperature rises; the solubility of gases generally decreases.

explain.title: Crystallization can purify a solid
explain.body: A substance such as potassium nitrate can be dissolved in hot water, and the solution can be cooled to form crystals. Filtering, washing and drying the crystals separates the purified solid from soluble impurities.

explain.title: Structure explains useful properties
explain.body: Graphite feels slippery because its layers slide over one another, while a diamond's high refractive index contributes to its brilliance. Graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms and is useful in electronics because of its electrical properties.

mistakes: Do not confuse plasma with an ordinary gas: plasma contains ionized particles.
Do not call every mixture a solution; suspensions and colloids have dispersed particles.
When defining solubility, include the temperature and the saturated-solution condition.
Do not say all solutes respond to heating in the same way: most solids become more soluble, while gases generally become less soluble.
For crystallization, do not cool before dissolving the impure solid in hot water and filtering the solution.
Do not describe graphene as many layers; it is a single layer, while graphite consists of stacked layers.
When comparing coal with diamond, distinguish impure amorphous coal from crystalline diamond.
In branch questions, choose the branch by the focus of the topic, not just by the name of a substance.
